Three things happened for Ramp investors on the same day:
The good news:
Brex essentially acknowledged Ramp won, even if they aren’t 100% direct competitors in every segment and with every product today. Started later, doing $1 billion to Brex’s $700 million.
The uncomfortable news:
When real money—not a secondary buyer purchasing 2% of the cap table—wrote an actual check for the whole asset, they valued it at 7x revenue. If you multiply Ramp’s billion-dollar run rate by 7, you get $7 billion. Even doubling it for faster growth gets you to $15 billion. Ramp raised at $32 billion.
The structural news:
Capital One now owns both Discover (closed for $50 billion) and Brex. Discover has a closed network—meaning Cap One captures all the interchange instead of splitting it with Visa and Mastercard. They can now route Brex spend onto their own rails.
If you’re Ramp, you’re now playing against the A-team with a structural cost advantage.
The mark-to-market conversation is going to be awkward: How do you factor in a comparable transaction at 7x revenue when your last round implied 30x?

hubristic fundraising
. And we should probably talk about it. Because hubristic fundraising is back. In a big way. It was back big time in 2025 and is back even bigger time in 2026. First, What Is Hubristic Fundraising? Take a valuation that requires Top 0.1%+ annual growth for a decade to grow into
Raise at 100x-500x+ revenue multiple. Often, again and again. Build your entire talent acquisition, press strategy, and customer pitch around being “the most valuable” or “fastest-growing”

There’s a lot of debate on social media whether you can make your VP of Sales successful if they aren’t “hands on” — i.e., don’t want to sell themselves. I’m not sure this matters so much anymore. They often prefer to talk to humans than chatbots, which isn’t going away anytime soon. But what does matter:

Or perhaps your product is complicated, and you need someone with experience managing multiple stakeholders to get things done.

traces.answer: So my general advice on when to hire another head of sales (and/or sales execs) is if you want to double your revenues next year -- you need to make sure you can hire at least one good rep a month, and ideally two per month, once you have some scale. That’s generally about 12 reps a year for now. And if you’re growing quickly, that likely means 2-3 sales leaders over time. But I’ve also learned that a great VP of Sales will often start with just 1 great rep they know well. At first, this won’t seem like enough help. It rarely seems to be “enough” at first. Then later, she’ll bring in a few more reps under her. This doesn’t always happen overnight. But in many cases, what happens is the first new sales leader gets amazing results — then struggles after that. She brought in too many reps before she could properly manage them all herself. Or maybe they weren't truly great. So I think you can go either way here. You can criticize someone if they aren't recruiting any more folks. Maybe most of us will. But we shouldn't judge those that get going with just 1 great rep under them. Because that's how it starts.

So I've been lucky enough over the years to meet so many incredible VPs of Sales. And you know what? Incredibly, some just fail no matter how much they try. They can't close even after trying for months. It happens. Now when this happens, I think it's fair to criticize a VP of Sales once they have failed for quite some time (e.g., 90 days) if they aren't improving things. You don't need to go nuclear on social media, but you need to call out that failure. But then you gotta move on. If nothing else, hire another great VP of Sales. Because most importantly, you're losing precious time. Time where leads could be converted to customers. To revenue. So why would you wait longer than 60-90 days to make any change here?

So I've talked on SaaStr for years now about how important it is to hire a great VP of Sales. And what happens when you don't. When you make this mistake by not hiring someone truly strong in your early days, especially with the headcount budget that you probably will start off with, it doesn't help. It makes things worse.
First, if you're growing quickly, you'll end up spending all your precious money on mediocre reps. If you can just spend half that money on one or two very good ones, they'll do far, far better than any bunch of mediocre folks. Second, you'll never get out of the hole. Because these mediocre reps won't ever hit quota, so no matter how much time goes by, nothing will really change. Third, your leads will dwindle, because if the VP isn't good enough, she or he won't know how to properly leverage marketing and generate interest and excitement. So over time, your funnel dries down. Fourth, morale will plummet. Everyone sees these poor performers flailing, and everyone knows why we aren't getting anywhere. Fifth, you'll lose credibility. You simply can't attract the best talent if you've made too many mis-hires. Sixth, and most importantly -- even if you were doing OK before, after an unhappy stretch under a bad VP of Sales... you'll never get past $10m-$15m ARR. That's where the "economy of scale" kicks in. You'll never figure it out. No matter how hard you try. Now some of my top learnings here:

A great VP of Sales is worth her weight in gold. But also — a great VP of Sales needs a bit of help herself. She can’t single-handedly fix everything. They need a few key pieces of support to succeed. Most importantly, they need some space to run. Not endless space. But some space to run. Otherwise, they’ll fail fast, or slow, depending on how long it takes them to realize they’re being micromanaged.

So who said that AI means everything in SaaS needs to be a personalized experience?
There’s been this narrative that you need to use AI to personalize your entire product and everything in your business to every single one of your customers. I don’t think that’s true. You should start with what matters most. Start with where it actually makes an impact. Because if we’re honest, it does feel like there’s so much noise out there right now. And everyone’s saying you got to personalize your whole thing, you gotta put your logo everywhere, you gotta put your logo in your email signature. Maybe just pick two things that matter. Pick two things that really matter. That you can do well with AI. And then go deep. Go deep there. Don’t spread yourself too thin. There’s enough energy and effort already.
